sections.title: Start here
sections.body:
Mechanics of materials looks inside a loaded part. Stress is how hard the material is being pushed or pulled per unit of area. Strain is how much it deforms in response.

Four loadings cover the topic: pulling along the length, twisting, bending and shear. Each has one formula for stress and one for deformation.
pitfalls: Mixing units: stay in N, mm and MPa and the numbers work out.
Reading the maximum moment at midspan when the load is not symmetric. The peak is where shear crosses zero.

tips.from: Mark Mattson, FE Mechanics of Materials Review Session 2022
items: Draw a shear diagram by following the loads from left to right.
For a symmetric section the neutral axis is at mid-depth. For any other section find the centroid first.
Handbook search is literal. Searching 'torsion' finds the section; 'torsional' may not.
N against kN and mm against m cause most wrong answers; an answer off by orders of magnitude is a units slip.
On Mohr's circle an angle is twice the angle on the element.
The tension side of a beam is where reinforcement goes in concrete, so know which face is in tension.

bridge.plain: Mechanics of materials asks what happens inside a member that carries load: how hard the material is being pulled, squeezed or sheared (stress), and how much it stretches or bends (strain and deflection).
core: Stress is force divided by area. Strain is change in length divided by length.
For most materials stress = stiffness × strain, until yielding.
A beam carries load by bending: the top squeezes and the bottom stretches, or the reverse.
Shear and moment diagrams show the internal forces along a beam.
bridge.links: It needs statics to get the internal forces. Structural design (steel and concrete) and the strength of soils in geotechnics build on it.
bridge.exam: Work in newtons and millimetres so stresses come out in megapascals, or in kips and inches for ksi.

sections.title: Shear and moment diagrams
sections.body:
Shear and moment diagrams show the internal force and bending along a beam. Shear is the tendency of one part of the beam to slide past the next. Moment is the tendency to bend.

Build them from left to right. A point load makes the shear jump by the load. A uniform load makes the shear slope steadily. The moment at any point is the area under the shear diagram up to that point. The moment peaks where the shear crosses zero. Memorize the common cases: they save time.
pitfalls: Assuming the maximum moment is at midspan when the loading is not symmetric.
Stopping at the first shear area. Work out the moment at every point of zero shear and compare magnitudes.
Drawing a positive moment for a cantilever under downward load. It is negative along the whole length and zero at the free end.

example.problem: A simply supported beam spans 4 m with 12 kN/m. Find the maximum shear and moment.
example.steps:
V_{max} = \frac{12(4)}{2} = 24 kN at the supports.

M_{max} = \frac{12(4)^{2}}{8} = 24 kN·m at midspan.

ideas.title: Shear height is moment slope
ideas.text: The value of the shear diagram at any section equals the slope of the moment diagram there. Where the shear passes through zero the moment is at a peak, and where the shear jumps at a support the moment diagram has a kink.

ideas.title: Shapes that go together
ideas.text: A point load gives a step in the shear and a straight-line moment. A uniform load gives a sloping shear and a parabolic moment. With no load between two points the shear is constant.

ideas.title: Moment from shear areas
ideas.text: The change in moment between two sections is the area under the shear diagram between them. For point loads and uniform loads these areas are rectangles and triangles, so no integration is needed. Under a uniform load w, the shear reaches zero a distance V / w from where it has the value V.

ideas.title: Sketch the deflected shape
ideas.text: A beam that sags has positive moment, with tension on the bottom. A beam that hogs, as over a support or along a cantilever, has negative moment, with tension on top. Where the curvature reverses, the moment passes through zero.

ideas.title: Shearing force and bending moment
ideas.text: For a simply supported beam under full uniform load, shear is zero at midspan, so the moment peaks there: M_{max} = w L^{2} / 8. It equals the area under the shear diagram from the support to midspan.

ideas.title: Shearing force and bending moment
ideas.text: Shear is largest where the beam meets its supports and equals the reaction there. For a full uniform load each reaction is w L / 2, and shear falls linearly to zero at midspan.

examples.problem: A simply supported beam spans 12 m and carries a uniform load of 15 kN/m over its full length. What is the maximum bending moment?
examples.idea: For a simply supported beam under full uniform load, shear is zero at midspan, so the moment peaks there: M_{max} = w L^{2} / 8. It equals the area under the shear diagram from the support to midspan.
examples.steps:
Reaction = 15(12) / 2 = 90 kN.

M_{max} = \frac{w L^{2}}{8} = \frac{15(12)^{2}}{8} = 270 kN·m, at midspan.

examples.problem: A beam rests on supports A and B, 8 m apart, and overhangs 2.2 m beyond B. It carries 19 kN at 4 m from A and 6 kN at the tip of the overhang. What is the largest bending moment magnitude in the beam?
examples.idea: The moment peaks where the shear changes sign: under the load in the span and over support B. The moment at B is simply the overhang load times its arm, and it is negative. Compare the two magnitudes.
examples.steps:
Moment at B = -6(2.2) = -13.2 kN·m.

Reaction at A = \frac{19(8 - 4) - 6(2.2)}{8} = 7.850 kN, so the moment under the span load = 7.850 × 4 = 31.4 kN·m.

The larger magnitude is 31.4 kN·m.

examples.problem: The shear diagram of a beam starts at +30 kN at the left support, where the moment is zero, and falls in a straight line to -20 kN at a point 7 m away. What is the maximum bending moment in that length?
examples.idea: The moment is greatest where the shear crosses zero. Similar triangles locate the crossing, and the moment there is the area of the positive shear triangle.
examples.steps:
Zero shear at 7 × \frac{30}{30 + 20} = 4.20 m from the support.

M_{max} = \frac{1}{2}(30)(4.20) = 63.00 kN·m.

sections.deep:
Shear and moment diagrams show the internal forces along a beam. They are linked by calculus: the slope of the shear diagram is the negative of the load intensity, and the slope of the moment diagram is the shear. So shear is constant where there is no load and linear under a uniform load, while moment is linear where shear is constant and parabolic where shear is linear.

The maximum moment occurs where shear is zero or changes sign. A point load makes shear jump; a couple makes moment jump. The change in moment between two points equals the area under the shear diagram between them.
method: Find the reactions.
Start at the left end and track shear: jump at point loads, slope under distributed loads.
Locate where shear crosses zero.
Compute the moment there as the area under the shear diagram up to that point.
Check that shear and moment return to zero at free or simply supported ends.

sections.primer: Inside a loaded beam there are two internal effects at every section: a shear force, which tries to slide one side past the other, and a bending moment, which bends the beam. A shear diagram and a moment diagram plot these along the beam, starting from the support reactions.

terms: shear force
the internal force that acts across a beam's section, trying to slide one part past the other
bending moment
the internal turning effect at a beam's section that makes the beam curve
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
reaction
the force a support pushes back with to hold a structure in place
couple
two equal and opposite forces a distance apart; together they only turn an object and do not push it anywhere
cantilever
a beam held rigidly at one end and free at the other, like a diving board or a signal mast arm
simply supported
resting on a pin at one end and a roller at the other, so the ends can rotate freely

sections.title: Stresses and strains
sections.body:
Stress is internal force per unit area. Strain is deformation per unit length. In the elastic range they are proportional, linked by the modulus of elasticity.

Each kind of loading has its own stress formula. Axial load gives uniform normal stress. Bending gives normal stress that is zero at the neutral axis and largest at the outer edge. Torsion gives shear stress that is largest at the outer surface of a shaft. Transverse shear in a beam peaks at the neutral axis. A restrained bar that is heated develops thermal stress.

formulas.name: Restrained thermal stress
formulas.expr: stress = E × expansion coefficient × temperature change

pitfalls: Mixing units. N and mm give MPa directly.
Using the diameter instead of the radius for the outer fibre distance.
Forgetting to halve the force for a bolt in double shear, which doubles the stress.
Mixing lb with kips, or ft^{2} with in^{2}. An answer wrong by a factor of 1,000 or 144 is a unit slip.
Reading a force as kN when the work was in N and mm. With stresses in MPa and lengths in mm, forces come out in N.

ideas.text: Stress = E × strain is F = k x with force divided by area and stretch divided by length. Strain has no units, and it can be found from stress and E alone, without the member's length.

ideas.title: Average shear in a pin or bolt
ideas.text: Average shear stress is the force on one shear plane divided by the bolt's cross-section. A bolt through a clevis is cut on two planes, so each plane carries half the load.

ideas.title: Uniaxial loading
ideas.text: Average normal stress is force divided by the cross-sectional area perpendicular to the force. With newtons and square millimetres the result is in MPa.

ideas.title: Stresses in beams
ideas.text: Bending stress varies linearly from zero at the neutral axis to a maximum at the extreme fibre: stress = M c / I = M / S. For a rectangle the section modulus is S = b h^{2} / 6.

ideas.title: Torsion
ideas.text: Torsional shear stress in a circular shaft grows linearly with radius: stress = T r / J. For a solid shaft J = π d^{4} / 32, so the maximum, at the surface, is 16 T / (π d^{3}).

ideas.title: Thermal deformations
ideas.text: A free bar would lengthen by (coefficient × temperature change × L). The walls prevent that, which is the same as compressing the bar by the same strain. Stress = E × coefficient × temperature change, independent of length and area.

sections.deep:
Stress is force per unit area and strain is deformation per unit length. Normal stress acts perpendicular to a surface and shear stress acts along it. In the elastic range they are proportional: normal stress = E × strain, shear stress = G × shear strain, with G = E / (2(1 + Poisson's ratio)).

Each loading has its own formula: P / A for axial load, M c / I for bending, T r / J for torsion of round shafts, V Q / (I b) for transverse shear, p r / t for thin pressure vessels. Recognising the loading is most of the work.
method: Identify the loading: axial, bending, torsion, shear or pressure.
Compute the section property the formula needs: A, I, J or Q.
Work in N, mm and MPa, or lb, in and psi.
Find the location of maximum stress: extreme fibre for bending, outer surface for torsion, neutral axis for shear.
Compare with the allowable stress if asked, using the factor of safety.

sections.primer: Stress is how hard the material is working: force divided by the area that carries it. Pulling gives tension, pushing gives compression, sliding gives shear. Strain is how much the material deforms: change in length divided by original length. Bending and twisting give stresses that are largest at the outer surface.

terms: strain
change in length divided by original length; it has no units
modulus of elasticity
the stiffness of a material: stress divided by strain while the material still springs back
normal stress
force per unit area acting perpendicular to a surface; tension pulls apart, compression pushes together
neutral axis
the line through a bent beam's section where the material is neither stretched nor squeezed
torsion
twisting of a member about its own long axis
shear stress
force per unit area acting parallel to a surface, trying to slide one layer over the next
poisson's ratio
how much a bar thins sideways compared with how much it stretches lengthways
section modulus

sections.title: Deformations
sections.body:
Loaded parts change shape. A bar in tension gets longer, a shaft in torsion twists, and a beam in bending deflects. The amount depends on the load, the length, the size of the cross-section and the stiffness of the material.

The axial and torsional formulas have the same form: load times length over stiffness. Beam deflections come from tabulated cases in the handbook. Temperature changes cause free expansion in proportion to length and temperature change.

formulas.name: Thermal deformation
formulas.expr: change in length = expansion coefficient × L × temperature change

pitfalls: Entering E in GPa with other values in N and mm. Convert GPa to MPa by multiplying by 1,000.
Leaving the angle of twist in radians when the choices are in degrees. Multiply by 180 / π.
Using E where G is needed. Twist and torsional shear use the shear modulus G.

example.problem: A 3 m aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa) with a 200 mm^{2} cross-section carries 14 kN. How much does it stretch?

ideas.title: Uniaxial loading and deformation

ideas.title: Thermal deformations

sections.deep:
Deformation follows from stress through the material's stiffness. An axial member changes length by P L / (A E), a shaft twists by T L / (G J) and a temperature change causes a strain of the expansion coefficient times the temperature change. Members in series add their deformations; members in parallel share load in proportion to their stiffness.

When a structure is restrained so that it cannot deform freely, the problem is statically indeterminate and needs a compatibility equation: the deformations must fit the supports. Beam deflections come from the handbook's table and can be superposed.
method: Write the deformation formula for each segment.
For members in series, add the segment deformations.
For a restrained system, write the free deformation, then the deformation caused by the unknown restraining force, and set their sum to the allowed movement.
Solve for the force, then the stress.
Check units, keeping E in MPa with N and mm.

sections.primer: Members change shape under load. A bar under tension gets longer, a beam sags, a shaft twists and a heated bar expands. Each has a formula with the load on top and a stiffness underneath: a stiffer material or a bigger section deforms less.

strain
change in length divided by original length; it has no units
statically indeterminate

polar moment of inertia
the measure of a cross-section's resistance to twisting
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
moment of inertia
a measure of how far an area's material is spread from an axis; the larger it is, the stiffer the shape in bending about that axis

sections.title: Combined stresses, principal stresses and Mohr's circle
sections.body:
At a point, the stresses you see depend on the direction you look. Rotate the element and the normal and shear stresses change. At one orientation the shear disappears and the normal stresses reach their largest and smallest values: the principal stresses.

Mohr's circle is a picture of all those orientations. Its centre is the average of the two normal stresses and its radius comes from half their difference and the shear stress. The principal stresses are centre plus and minus radius. The maximum in-plane shear equals the radius. Thin-walled pressure vessels are a common application.
pitfalls: Using the full difference of the normal stresses instead of half of it in the radius.
Adding the axial and bending stresses without checking which face is in tension.
Forgetting that an angle on Mohr's circle is twice the angle on the element.

example.problem: A point has stresses of 60 MPa and 0 MPa on perpendicular faces with 40 MPa shear. Find the principal stresses.
example.steps:

ideas.title: Combined axial and bending stress
ideas.text: An eccentric load is an axial force plus a moment. The axial part gives P / A across the whole section. The bending part gives M c / I, tension on one face and compression on the other. Add them with their signs at the point asked about.

ideas.title: Mohr's circle by Pythagoras
ideas.text: The centre is the average of the two normal stresses. The radius is the hypotenuse of a triangle whose sides are half the difference of the normal stresses and the shear stress. Principal stresses are centre plus and minus radius, and the maximum in-plane shear equals the radius.

ideas.title: Mohr's circle
ideas.text: Principal stresses are the largest and smallest normal stresses at a point, found on the planes where shear is zero. On Mohr's circle the centre is the average normal stress and the radius is the square root of ((difference/2)^{2} + shear^{2}); the maximum principal stress is centre + radius.

ideas.title: Mohr's circle
ideas.text: The maximum in-plane shear stress is the radius of Mohr's circle, half the difference between the principal stresses. Compression is negative, so a tension and a compression add when you take the difference.

ideas.title: Cylindrical pressure vessel
ideas.text: In a thin-walled cylinder the circumferential (hoop) stress is p r / t and the longitudinal stress is p r / (2 t). The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, which is why such vessels split along their length.

examples.problem: At a point in a plate, the normal stresses on two perpendicular faces are 60 MPa and -60 MPa (tension positive). The shear stress on those faces is 80 MPa. What is the maximum principal stress?
examples.idea: Principal stresses are the largest and smallest normal stresses at a point, found on the planes where shear is zero. On Mohr's circle the centre is the average normal stress and the radius is the square root of ((difference/2)^{2} + shear^{2}); the maximum principal stress is centre + radius.
examples.steps:
Centre = \frac{60 + (-60)}{2} = 0 MPa.

Radius = \sqrt{(\frac{60 - (-60)}{2})^{2} + 80^{2}} = 100 MPa.

Maximum principal stress = 0 + 100 = 100 MPa.

examples.problem: A thin-walled cylindrical tank has a radius of 900 mm and a wall thickness of 18 mm. The internal pressure is 1.6 MPa. What is the hoop stress in the wall?
examples.idea: In a thin-walled cylinder the circumferential (hoop) stress is p r / t and the longitudinal stress is p r / (2 t). The hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, which is why such vessels split along their length.
examples.steps: Hoop stress = \frac{p r}{t} = \frac{1.6(900)}{18} = 80 MPa. The longitudinal stress is half of that, 40 MPa.

examples.problem: A square column 125 mm on a side carries a compressive load of 24 kN applied 325 mm from its centroid, on one axis of symmetry. What is the maximum tensile stress on the cross-section?
examples.idea: An eccentric load is an axial force plus a moment P e. The axial part compresses the whole section by P / A. The bending part adds M c / I in compression on the loaded side and in tension on the far side.
examples.steps:
Axial: \frac{24,000}{15,625} = 1.536 MPa compression.

Bending: \frac{M c}{I} = \frac{6 P e}{b^{3}} = \frac{6(24,000)(325)}{125^{3}} = 23.962 MPa.

Far face: 23.962 - 1.536 = 22.43 MPa tension.

examples.problem: A thin-walled cylindrical tank with closed ends has a radius of 575 mm and a wall thickness of 8 mm. The internal pressure is 1.4 MPa. What is the longitudinal (axial) stress in the wall?
examples.idea: The pressure on the end cap, p π r^{2}, is carried by the wall's ring of area 2π r t, giving p r / (2t). The hoop stress, p r / t, is twice as large, which is why pipes split lengthwise.

examples.problem: A bar carries a uniaxial tensile stress of 140 MPa. What is the shear stress on a plane whose normal makes 32° with the bar's axis?
examples.idea: On an inclined plane a uniaxial stress resolves into a normal part and a shear part. The shear stress is (stress) sin(angle) cos(angle), which peaks at half the axial stress on the 45° plane.

sections.deep:
Stress at a point depends on the orientation of the plane you look at. Rotating the element changes the normal and shear stresses, and Mohr's circle maps every orientation onto a circle. Its centre is the average normal stress and its radius is the maximum in-plane shear stress. The principal stresses are the largest and smallest normal stresses, where shear is zero, and sit at the ends of the horizontal diameter.

An angle on the element is doubled on the circle, so principal planes are 45° from maximum-shear planes. Combined loading problems simply add the stresses from each loading at the point before building the circle.
method: Find the stresses on the x and y faces at the point, adding the contributions of each loading.
Compute the centre: the average of the two normal stresses.
Compute the radius: square root of (half the difference)^{2} plus the shear stress squared.
Principal stresses are centre plus and minus radius; maximum in-plane shear is the radius.
Check: the two principal stresses must add up to the sum of the original normal stresses.

sections.primer: The stress at a point depends on the direction you look in. Turning an imaginary cut changes how much is normal stress and how much is shear. Mohr's circle is a picture that gives the stresses on every such cut, including the largest ones, the principal stresses.

terms: normal stress
force per unit area acting perpendicular to a surface; tension pulls apart, compression pushes together
mohr's circle
a circle drawn on stress axes that shows the normal and shear stress on every plane through a point
principal stress
the largest and smallest normal stresses at a point, found on the planes where shear stress is zero
shear stress
force per unit area acting parallel to a surface, trying to slide one layer over the next
moment
the turning effect of a force about a point: the force times its perpendicular distance from that point
